exam.subtitle: Eigenvalues, Diagonalization and Linear Spaces
exam.instructions: Complete all tasks. Show complete solution approach for all calculations. Permitted aids: calculator without programming function. Good luck!

exercises.title: Gaussian Algorithm and Solvability
exercises.description:
Given is the linear system of equations:
`\begin{align}
2x_1 + 3x_2 - x_3 &= 5 \\
x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 &= 1 \\
3x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 &= 6
\end{align}`

a) Solve the system using the Gaussian algorithm.
b) Determine the rank of the coefficient matrix.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Set up augmented matrix
`\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c}
2 & 3 & -1 & 5 \\
1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\
3 & 2 & 1 & 6
\end{array}\right)`

Step 2: First elimination (row 1 as pivot)
Swap rows 1 and 2 for better pivot:
`\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\
2 & 3 & -1 & 5 \\
3 & 2 & 1 & 6
\end{array}\right)`

Step 5: Back substitution
From row 2: `5x_2 - 5x_3 = 3 \Rightarrow x_2 = x_3 + \frac{3}{5}`
From row 1: `x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 = 1`
`x_1 = 1 + x_2 - 2x_3 = 1 + (x_3 + \frac{3}{5}) - 2x_3 = \frac{8}{5} - x_3`

Step 6: General solution
`x_3 = t` (free parameter)
`x_2 = t + \frac{3}{5}`
`x_1 = \frac{8}{5} - t`

Rank of coefficient matrix: `\text{rank}(A) = 2`

exercises.title: Eigenvalues of a 2×2 Matrix
exercises.description:
Given is the matrix `A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}`.

a) Determine all eigenvalues of A.
b) Calculate the corresponding eigenvectors.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Set up characteristic polynomial
`\det(A - \lambda I) = \det\begin{pmatrix} 3-\lambda & 1 \\ 2 & 2-\lambda \end{pmatrix}`
`= (3-\lambda)(2-\lambda) - 1 \cdot 2`
`= 6 - 3\lambda - 2\lambda + \lambda^2 - 2`
`= \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 4`

Step 2: Calculate eigenvalues
`\lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 4 = 0`
Using the quadratic formula:
`\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{25-16}}{2} = \frac{5 \pm 3}{2}`
`\lambda_1 = 4`, `\lambda_2 = 1`

Step 3: Eigenvector for λ₁ = 4
`(A - 4I)v = 0`:
`\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`
From first row: `-v_1 + v_2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = v_1`
Eigenvector: `v^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}`

Step 4: Eigenvector for λ₂ = 1
`(A - I)v = 0`:
`\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`
From first row: `2v_1 + v_2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = -2v_1`
Eigenvector: `v^{(2)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}`

Step 5: Answer
Eigenvalues: `\lambda_1 = 4`, `\lambda_2 = 1`
Eigenvectors: `v^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}`, `v^{(2)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}`

exercises.title: Diagonalization of a 3×3 Matrix
exercises.description:
Given is the matrix `B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}`.

a) Check whether B is diagonalizable.
b) If yes, give a diagonal matrix D and a transformation matrix P such that `P^{-1}BP = D`.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Characteristic polynomial
`\det(B - \lambda I) = \det\begin{pmatrix} 1-\lambda & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{pmatrix}`
Expansion along second row:
`= (2-\lambda) \cdot \det\begin{pmatrix} 1-\lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{pmatrix}`
`= (2-\lambda)[(1-\lambda)^2 - 1]`
`= (2-\lambda)(\lambda^2 - 2\lambda) = (2-\lambda)\lambda(\lambda-2) = -\lambda(2-\lambda)^2`

Step 2: Eigenvalues
`\lambda_1 = 0` (simple), `\lambda_2 = 2` (double)

Step 3: Eigenvector for λ₁ = 0
`(B - 0I)v = Bv = 0`:
`\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`
From row 2: `2v_2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = 0`
From row 1: `v_1 + v_3 = 0 \Rightarrow v_3 = -v_1`
Eigenvector: `v^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}`

Step 4: Eigenvectors for λ₂ = 2
`(B - 2I)v = 0`:
`\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`
From row 1: `-v_1 + v_3 = 0 \Rightarrow v_3 = v_1`
`v_2` is freely choosable.
Eigenvectors: `v^{(2)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}`, `v^{(3)} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`

Step 5: Check diagonalizability
Dimension of eigenspace for `\lambda = 2`: `\dim(E_2) = 2` = algebraic multiplicity
Since we have 3 linearly independent eigenvectors, B is diagonalizable.

Step 6: Transformation matrix and diagonal matrix
`P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}`, `D = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}`
It holds: `P^{-1}BP = D`

exercises.title: Basis and Dimension
exercises.description:
Given are the vectors in `\mathbb{R}^3`:
`v_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}`, `v_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}`, `v_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}`, `v_4 = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}`

a) Check whether vectors `v_1, v_2, v_3` are linearly independent.
b) Determine a basis of the subspace spanned by `\{v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4\}`.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Check linear independence of v₁, v₂, v₃
We solve `\alpha_1 v_1 + \alpha_2 v_2 + \alpha_3 v_3 = 0`:
`\alpha_1 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha_2 \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha_3 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`

Step 2: Set up system of equations
`\begin{align}
\alpha_1 + 2\alpha_2 + \alpha_3 &= 0 \\
2\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 - \alpha_3 &= 0 \\
\alpha_1 + 3\alpha_2 + 2\alpha_3 &= 0
\end{align}`
Matrix: `\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}`

Step 4: Back substitution
From row 2: `\alpha_2 + \alpha_3 = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha_2 = -\alpha_3`
From row 1: `\alpha_1 + 2(-\alpha_3) + \alpha_3 = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha_1 = \alpha_3`
Only the trivial solution `\alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \alpha_3 = 0` exists.
`\Rightarrow v_1, v_2, v_3` are linearly independent.

Step 5: Basis of spanned subspace
We check whether `v_4` is linearly dependent on `v_1, v_2, v_3`:
`v_4 = \beta_1 v_1 + \beta_2 v_2 + \beta_3 v_3`
`\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = \beta_1 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \beta_2 \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + \beta_3 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}`

Step 6: Solve the system
`\begin{align}
\beta_1 + 2\beta_2 + \beta_3 &= 3 \\
2\beta_1 + \beta_2 - \beta_3 &= 3 \\
\beta_1 + 3\beta_2 + 2\beta_3 &= 4
\end{align}`
Solution: `\beta_1 = 1, \beta_2 = 1, \beta_3 = 0`
`\Rightarrow v_4 = v_1 + v_2`
Since `v_4` is linearly dependent, `\{v_1, v_2, v_3\}` forms a basis of the subspace.
Dimension: 3

exercises.title: Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization
exercises.description:
Given are the vectors in `\mathbb{R}^3`:
`u_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`, `u_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}`, `u_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}`

Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to construct an orthonormal basis.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Normalize first vector
`v_1 = u_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`
`||v_1|| = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + 0^2} = \sqrt{2}`
`e_1 = \frac{v_1}{||v_1||} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`

Step 2: Orthogonalize second vector
`v_2 = u_2 - \langle u_2, e_1 \rangle e_1`
`\langle u_2, e_1 \rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}`
`v_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}`

Step 3: Normalize second vector
`||v_2|| = \sqrt{(\frac{1}{2})^2 + (-\frac{1}{2})^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} + 1} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}`
`e_2 = \frac{v_2}{||v_2||} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{pmatrix}`

Step 4: Orthogonalize third vector
`v_3 = u_3 - \langle u_3, e_1 \rangle e_1 - \langle u_3, e_2 \rangle e_2`
`\langle u_3, e_1 \rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}`
`\langle u_3, e_2 \rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}`

Step 5: Calculate v₃
`v_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{pmatrix}`
`= \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{6} \\ -\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{1}{3} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \end{pmatrix}`

Step 6: Normalize third vector
`||v_3|| = \sqrt{\frac{4}{9} + \frac{4}{9} + \frac{4}{9}} = \sqrt{\frac{4}{3}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}`
`e_3 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\begin{pmatrix} -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{pmatrix}`

Orthonormal basis: `\left\{\begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{pmatrix}\right\}`
